title: Introducing Securing America’s Infrastructure Foundation | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z has incubated Securing America’s Infrastructure Foundation (SAIF), a 501(c)(3) nonprofit led by Anne Neuberger that will deliver free AI-based cybersecurity software, training and incident response to under-resourced public institutions such as small municipalities, school districts and rural hospitals. It starts with a two-city pilot and $25 million in committed funding from a16z's founding partners, aiming for 5-10 anchor cities over five years.

themes.theme: Under-resourced public institutions as the cyber front line

insights.claim: Ransomware attacks on small U.S. public institutions, such as county 911 dispatch, school districts and rural hospitals, happen regularly, and the victims rarely have the budget, staff or technical bench to defend themselves.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Small public entities are a large, underserved attack surface and a potential market for cheap, managed cyber defense.
insights.quote: These aren’t hypotheticals — they are a regular occurrence across the United States, and the institutions absorbing the damage rarely have the budget, staff, or technical bench to defend themselves.
insights.locator: America’s small cities are on the front lines

insights.claim: Rural hospitals sometimes pay six-figure ransoms they cannot afford because paying costs less than losing patient care for a week, which shows how ransomware economics push under-defended victims to pay.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Rational ransom-paying by critical-service providers sustains ransomware profitability; prevention capacity is the lever.
insights.quote: A rural hospital pays a six-figure ransom it can’t afford because paying is cheaper than losing patient care for a week.
insights.locator: America’s small cities are on the front lines

insights.claim: According to Neuberger, from her NSA and White House cyber roles, the institutions that hold communities' most sensitive data and systems (student records, patient files, water systems, emergency services) are consistently the least resourced to protect them.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Risk and defensive capability are inversely distributed across U.S. infrastructure, creating a systemic weak link.
insights.quote: the same institutions expected to protect the most sensitive data and systems in our communities — student records, patient files, water systems, emergency services — are the least resourced to do it.
insights.locator: I spent the last several years

insights.claim: SAIF plans to focus on specific critical sectors such as the roughly 1,800 rural U.S. hospitals, which are often the only providers of critical services in their communities.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Single-provider institutions carry concentrated community risk, so a breach there has outsized local impact.
insights.quote: the nation’s 1,800 rural hospitals for example – that provide critical services to communities where they are the only providers.

themes.theme: AI divide between well-resourced and small institutions

insights.claim: AI is improving productivity, diagnostics and cyber defense at well-resourced organizations but is largely bypassing small public institutions, not because it doesn't apply but because it may not be accessible, affordable or practical for them.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: AI may widen the gap in security and service quality between large and small institutions unless delivery models change.
insights.quote: the AI wave that is improving productivity, diagnostics, and cyber defense in well-resourced organizations is largely passing these institutions by.
insights.locator: I spent the last several years

insights.claim: Ben Horowitz argues that in parts of America, social infrastructure such as hospitals and municipal services lacks the resources or training to capture AI's benefits and may bear more of its risks.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz
insights.so_what: a16z frames uneven AI access as a fairness and security problem, which supports its public-benefit positioning on AI.
insights.quote: where the social infrastructure, hospitals, municipal services don’t have the resources or training to get the benefits of AI, and may bear more of the risks.
insights.locator: We believe that the best thing

insights.claim: The Foundation starts with AI-based cybersecurity because cyberattacks are growing more sophisticated and AI is a game changer for defense, for example by finding and fixing vulnerabilities in code for devices like MRI machines and hospital monitors.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: AI-driven vulnerability discovery and remediation in medical and embedded devices is singled out as a high-value defensive use case.
insights.quote: using AI to find and fix vulnerabilities in code for devices like MRI machines or hospital monitors

insights.claim: Securing America’s Infrastructure Foundation (SAIF) is a new 501(c)(3) nonprofit incubated by a16z to deliver AI and cybersecurity tools, hands-on support and training to public institutions that lack access to AI tools.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: A major VC is moving into public-sector cyber capacity-building through a nonprofit vehicle.
insights.quote: Securing America’s Infrastructure Foundation (SAIF) is a new 501(c)(3) nonprofit, incubated by a16z, built to deliver AI and cybersecurity tools, hands-on support, and training

insights.claim: SAIF rejects a traditional grants model and will instead deliver software, hands-on training and cyber incident response at no cost, with experts embedded long enough to make the capability stick, which it likens to forward-deployed engineering.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: The bet is that capability transfer, not funding, is the binding constraint for small institutions' cyber defense.
insights.quote: The model is closer to “forward-deployed engineering” than philanthropy as usual

insights.claim: When choosing recipients, SAIF will weigh leadership buy-in, digital vulnerability, infrastructure readiness and the diversity of communities it can reach, on the view that such programs only work if built with the people they serve.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Leadership buy-in and readiness are treated as preconditions for public-sector tech adoption, not just need.
insights.quote: factors like leadership buy-in, digital vulnerability, infrastructure readiness, and the diversity of communities we can reach will be key.
insights.locator: Why cyber-defense and public benefit, first

insights.claim: SAIF's first-year scope is deliberately narrow (cybersecurity, digital literacy and responsible AI use for public benefit) because these are acknowledged to be hard problems.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Expect modest, focused early outcomes rather than broad public-sector AI deployment.
insights.quote: our first-year focus is deliberately narrow because we know these are hard problems: cybersecurity, digital literacy, and responsible AI use for public benefit.
insights.locator: Why cyber-defense and public benefit, first

insights.claim: SAIF will launch with a pilot in two small cities in different geographic regions, reflecting the view that ransomware, digital exclusion and underinvestment in public IT affect communities across America.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: The pilot is meant to test whether the model works across varied regions before it scales.
insights.quote: We will launch with a pilot in two small cities in different geographic regions

insights.claim: SAIF aims to reach roughly 5-10 anchor cities over five years, starting with $25 million in committed funding from a16z's founding partners.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: The scale is small relative to the problem, so this works more as a demonstration model and policy signal than a national fix.
insights.quote: We aim toward roughly 5-10 anchor cities over five years, beginning with $25 million in committed funding from a16z’s founding partners.

insights.claim: Anne Neuberger, a16z general partner and Head of Global Affairs and former NSA official and Deputy National Security Advisor for Cyber and Emerging Technology, will lead SAIF initially as a volunteer and later hire an executive director.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Former senior government cyber officials joining a16z gives the firm policy credibility and access in national-security tech.
insights.quote: I’m leading this effort and will initially run the nonprofit as a volunteer, establishing its strategy and building the founding team.

insights.claim: SAIF's board pairs enterprise and public-sector security veterans: Brian Barrios (CSO of Southern California Edison), Stephen Goldsmith (Harvard Kennedy School, former Mayor of Indianapolis and NYC Deputy Mayor), Bob Lord (ex-Twitter, Yahoo CISO, CISA), Vishal Misra (Columbia) and Phil Venables (ex-Goldman Sachs and Google Cloud CISO, now Ballistic Ventures).
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: The board is built to turn enterprise-grade defenses into practical tools for small institutions.
insights.quote: Phil Venables spent 17 years as Goldman Sachs’ first Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) and later became Google Cloud’s founding CISO
